extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, art students, and art critics interested in principles of painting and architecture (Victorian-era critical guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and producing painting and architecture, emphasizing balance of novelty, composition, naturalism, and moral/aesthetic temperament. Applies to makers and critics deciding whether work is art or mere manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture vs manufacture (rule-copying is not art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly so far as architecture works on known rules, and from given models, it is not an art, but a manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an architect merely copies capitals or mouldings from Phidias (or any given model) and follows legal/formal correctness alone, the result is manufacture not art. By analogy, copying heads and hands from Titian and calling oneself a painter is equally mechanical. True art requires departure from mere rule-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great art must say new and different things (novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art, whether expressing itself in words, colors, or stones, does not say the same thing over and over again; the merit ... consists in its saying new and different things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may require of an architect, as of a novelist, that he should be not only correct, but entertaining. Repetition and mere conformity to type are not signs of genius in marble any more than in print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety (change) is a necessity; monotony has limited use
rubrics_metrics.description: Change or variety is as much a necessity to the human heart and brain in buildings as in books; there is no merit, though there is some occasional use, in monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect pleasure and profit from architecture exhibiting variety; dislike architecture whose ornaments/pillars are all of one pattern. Use variety to enliven composition; monotony only occasionally useful to set up change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish healthy from diseased love of change
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between a healthy and a diseased love of change; the Gothic rose in healthy love of change and fell in part by diseased love of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy change yields subtle and delicate variation; diseased change repeats novelty so often that change itself becomes monotonous and drives the observer to extreme, fantastic degrees. Use variation judiciously, not continually for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotony should serve to give value to change (transparent monotony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotony in certain measure, used in order to give value to change, and, above all, that 'transparent' monotony which, like the shadows of a great painter, suffers all manner of dimly suggested form to be seen through the body of it, is an essential in architectural as in all other composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ 'transparent' monotony (subtle, allowing forms through it) so that change becomes more rewarding; think of musical repetition varied by enrichment, or long passages broken by a new theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience / endurance of monotony is an aesthetic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to the enjoyment of the change ... a certain degree of patience is required from the hearer or observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences/readers must be willing to endure some monotony (sometimes painful) as the price for the greater pleasure of eventual change; creators may rely on such endurance to build larger structural effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic capacity for perpetual novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic ... delighted in the infringement of every servile principle; and invented a series of forms of which the merit was, not merely that they were new, but that they were capable of perpetual novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural elements like the pointed arch, grouped shafts, and tracery admit endless variations (proportions changeable to infinity). Prefer forms that allow continuous, subtle invention rather than fixed, repeatable templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability / form follows practical use (Gothic virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic is ... the only rational architecture, as being that which can fit itself most easily to all services, vulgar or noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should submit to functional needs without losing unity or majesty: open windows where needed, add rooms or buttresses without slavish concern for imposed symmetry; practical necessity-driven variation often enhances interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should confess imperfection and desire change
rubrics_metrics.description: The first two elements of good architecture ... are the confession of Imperfection and the confession of Desire of Change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buildings should suggest that human work aspires and is incomplete; claiming absolute perfection degrades human art. Allow traces of development and change to remain as part of the edifice's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism vs arrangement: color and line have independent compositional value
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of colors and lines is an art analogous to the composition of music, and entirely independent of the representation of facts. Good coloring does not necessarily convey the image of anything but itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate color and line on their abstract relations (proportions of rays of light); a few masterful touches may be good coloring irrespective of whether they represent a dove's neck or other fact. Do not conflate faithful imitation with good composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noblest art unites abstract composition with imitative power
rubrics_metrics.description: The noblest art is an exact unison of the abstract value, with the imitative power, of forms and colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for works that are both formally noble (composition, color, line) and truthful to observed facts. Recognize that most minds excel in one or the other; only very few combine both perfectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three artist types: men of facts, men of design, and men of both
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are universally divided, as respects their artistical qualifications, into three great classes; on the right side are the men of facts, on the left the men of design, in the centre the men of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to situate practitioners and works: fact-workers supply truthful observation; designers supply compositional invention; central artists strive to combine both. Examples: Fig.1 (fact-work), Plate XIX (central), Fig.2 (design-focused).

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of facts despise design
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of facts despise design. This is the error of the common Dutch painters ... and other men who ... suppose that all is done when the imitation is perfected or sympathy expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware work that prizes mere faithful imitation (true tone, truthful skies) and rejects study of composition. Such practitioners often become presumptuous, incapable of admiring or learning from great designers, causing deadness of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of design despise facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of design despise facts. All noble design must deal with facts to a certain extent, for there is no food for it but in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ornamental invention that wilfully neglects natural truth—results become decrepit and lifeless (example: certain Chinese ornament). Good designers still take hints from nature for color and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of facts envy design (plagiarism/sterility)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of facts envy design ... having been taught that composition is the end of art, strive to obtain the inventive powers which nature has denied them ... perish in a fungous growth of plagiarism and laws of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not encourage imitative observers to attempt invention beyond their gifts by copying other designers; this leads to sterile plagiarism and harms the artistic community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of design envy facts (over-imitative ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of design envy facts; that is to say, when the temptation of closely imitating nature leads them to forget their own proper ornamental function ... they lose the power of composition for the sake of graphic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the ornamental and compositional role of design—avoid excessive literalism (example: hawthorn moulding at Bourges where imitation overruled ornamental judgment; the sculptor painting hawthorn green might have reduced work's compositional value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three moral-aesthetic classes: Purists, Naturalists, Sensualists
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall call, for convenience, Purists, Naturalists, and Sensualists ... The Purist does not mend nature, but receives from nature and from God that which is good for him; the Naturalist takes all home, and makes their cake of the one, and their couch of the other; the Sensualist fills himself with the husks that the swine did eat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to judge moral/aesthetic temper: Purists select the good and omit harshness; Naturalists render whole truth (good and evil) and can make it noble; Sensualists dwell upon evil/suffering for its own sake and are generally degraded. Examples: Angelico (Purist), Turner (Naturalist), Salvator Rosa/Caravaggio (Sensualists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess societal harm: errors of 'men of facts' more dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: The two morbid conditions to which the men of the inferior classes are liable ... the morbid state of men of facts injures the whole world. The morbid state of men of design injures themselves only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize criticism of fact-hunters who despise design or pursue imitation obsessively (they can become iconoclasts or cultural blinding forces). Example: attempts to force painters to falsify nature (Sir George Beaumont/Constable) are socially harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety can be distributed across features; seek compensatory variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the variety is in one feature, sometimes in another ... If the mouldings are constant, the surface sculpture will change; if the capitals are of a fixed design, the traceries will change ... the variety is found in the disposition of the masses, and in the figure sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing complex works, check that variety exists somewhere in the composition even if some elements are regularized. Balance constancy in one element with diversity in others (capitals vs traceries vs figure sculpture).
